newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - OPEC - Basking in a winter glow.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - OPEC - Basking in a winter glow.

text.p: OPEC ministers converged on Vienna on Monday for talks expected to freeze current output quotas to try to extend this year's rally in world oil prices.

Ali Nuaimi, minister of Saudi Arabia, the biggest exporter, who will have the decisive say, has yet to reach Vienna for a conference formally opening on Wednesday of the 11-nation Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries.

But delegates from some other cartel members who are already here predicted a consensus on extending existing quotas to mid-1997. Gulf sources suggest the Saudis also doubt if the market is strong enough yet to warrant turning up the taps.

OPEC Secretary-General Rilwanu Lukman of Nigeria expressed satisfaction at a rally that has already lifted prices to the highest since the 1991 Gulf War. An average of almost $20 per barrel so far this year is up $3 from 1995.
"It's cold but I hope it gets colder", Lukman told lobby reporters, observing that an early winter in the United States and Europe is firing up demand for fuel.
The U.S. trade deficit is widening. In another sign of the times, India's government says it is forced to consider a hike in state-subsidised petrol prices.

One reason for the tighter market is that new supply from non-OPEC sellers hasn't built up as fast as oil firms, who were content to operate with low stocks, had predicted. And there has been a delay implementing a food-for-oil accord to ease the U.N. Gulf War ban on Iraqi oil sales.
The higher prices add up to a windfall extra $30 billion in revenues for the 11 OPEC exporters whose economies were crimped in recent years when oil languished in the bargain basement.
Saudi Arabia, for instance, which produces a third of all cartel oil, can expect $10 billion of excess to deal with a projected 1996 deficit of almost $5 billion.

Given that it needs the money and that the bonanza may not last long, especially if Iraqi exports are allowed to resume in 1997, analysts doubt if Saudi Arabia is keen to raise production now and risk accelerating a likely decline in prices.
The Saudis' attitude is crucial because they are almost alone, with Gulf allies Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates, in having any appreciable unused production capacity.
Whilst the Saudis honoured an OPEC-mandated quota of 8.0 million barrels daily - they have 2.0 million in mothballs - most others are at capacity and several are violating quotas.

Quotas have not been officially raised since 1993, except for some extra volume pencilled in for Iraq. Yet even without this Iraqi oil, actual OPEC daily supply this year is about a million barrels above an agreed ceiling of 25.03 million.
Oil analysts say that if Saudi Arabia raised its output now on top of the cheating the price would almost certainly drop.

"There are some traders who know nothing else but that Saudi Arabia has a quota of eight million barrels per day so to some it would be bearish as hell for the Saudis to go up," said Vahan Zanoyan, a director at U.S.-based Petroleum Finance Corp.

U.N. diplomats said last week that the deal to ease sanctions on Iraq and let it sell oil for the first time since it invaded fellow OPEC founder member Kuwait in August 1990 could be implemented by the first quarter of 1997.
Benchmark Brent Blend crude oil traded in London just above $23 per barrel (42 US gallons) on Monday.
